transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-12-03 15:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (BrightMetrics Head of ML), Carlos Mendes (Infra), Leah Kim (PM)

Summary: Quick recap of last week's throughput tests, go over logs, tune batching and concurrency, plan next loads.

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining on a tight timeline, um, we wanted to cover the throughput tweaks from last week and then lock next tests. Samira, you want to kick off with the numbers?

[00:18] Samira Patel: yeah sure. I pushed the baseline runs again this morning. so to recap — the dedicated pool at 4 GPUs, model variant quantized int8, we saw about 650 tokens/sec aggregate at 50 concurrent sessions with our synthetic load, p95 latency around 420ms, p99 around 1.1s but that p99 was spiky due to occasional long tail kv misses.

[00:45] Priya Rao: sorry can I just interrupt — when you say kv misses, is that the prefix cache? because in our prod traffic we have a lot of repeated prefixes for the initial system prompts.

[01:00] Samira Patel: yep correct, kv == KV/prefix cache; the run had a cache hit rate of 78% which is lower than we'd expect once you get real traffic with repetition. we think improving hit rate to ~90% would cut p99 considerably.

[01:22] Carlos Mendes: curious — what's our concurrency pattern in that test? bursts or steady? because our frontend does a lot of bursty fan-out and that tends to queue up at the gateway and then slams the backend.

[01:35] Samira Patel: baseline test was steady at 50 conc but with short bursts every 20s to simulate user bursts; we didn't model the exact fan-out pattern you described. good call though, we should mirror your client fan-out.

[01:50] Leah Kim: from a product POV, our SLO is 95% of calls under 500ms and p99 under 1.2s. cost is also a constraint — we only have NTH-month budget to spend on dedicated GPUs, so we need to hit a sweet spot.

[02:10] Alex Chen: right — so the core tradeoff here is batching window vs latency. larger batching windows get you better throughput and lower per-token cost, but increase median/percentile latency. Samira had a suggestion to try 40ms continuous batching window instead of the current 80ms. Samira, walk us through expected results.

[02:28] Samira Patel: sure. with continuous batching at 40ms we expect smaller batches but higher request parallelism; preliminary sim shows token/sec drop of ~8% relative to 80ms, but p95 improves by ~15-20ms and p99 tails tighten because smaller windows avoid some tail serialization. importantly, while throughput dips, effective latency for most user flows meets your 500ms SLO. if we combine 40ms window with a higher KV cache TTL and better prefix dedup, we can get close to previous throughput while keeping latency low.

[03:05] Priya Rao: ok that sounds promising; do you have numbers for cost at those points? we need to show product and finance.

[03:12] Alex Chen: I'll attach an updated benchmark spreadsheet after the call. it will show per-model concurrency curves and estimated cost per 1M tokens for 40ms vs 80ms windows and with/without kv improvements.

[03:30] Carlos Mendes: another angle — queueing. right now our gateway has a naive queue that just accepts until queue depth hits 200, then backpressures. we were thinking of adding a token-bucket or shaping to smooth fan-outs. does Redwood support queueing policies at the route level?

[03:48] Samira Patel: yes — on Redwood Dedicated you can set per-route queueing policies, concurrency caps, and backpressure thresholds. we can also route burst traffic to a lower-cost warm pool to avoid impacting the hot path. in your case I'd suggest: 1) per-route concurrency cap at 30, 2) a short client-side retry with jitter, 3) a queue depth cap tuned to expected burst size. we can prototype those settings in the pilot env.

[04:20] Leah Kim: client-side retries worry me if p99 is already high — that could amplify load.

[04:28] Samira Patel: agreed — retries must be rate-limited and only for idempotent calls. another pattern is to prefer early rejection with a clear error code that signals the client to backoff, instead of blind retries.

[04:40] Priya Rao: quick question on concurrency targets — we're thinking of aiming for 8-12 concurrent requests per model shard in real traffic. how does that map to the pool sizing you suggested?

[04:53] Samira Patel: if you target 8-12 conc per shard and you have X shards per model (with a given layer parallelism), that translates to total concurrency on the pool. in our tests, 8 concurrent clients produced more stable p95 and lowered p99 tail when batching window was 40ms plus good cache hits. so we recommended an 8-client production-like run as next step.

[05:18] Carlos Mendes: ok so next test is 8 clients with the 40ms window and KV TTL bump; anything else for the run?

[05:25] Samira Patel: include tokenization samples from real logs — avg prompt size matters for batching and cost. Priya, can you send three representative prompt sets?

[05:34] Priya Rao: yes will do. will anonymize.

[05:38] Alex Chen: also we'll collect p50/p90/p95/p99, qps, tokens/sec, batch sizes, and kv hit rate. Samira will provide the run script so you can reproduce.

[05:50] Priya Rao: on security — Carlos, we still need SOC2/ISO docs to share with procurement. Carlos, can you get us contacts?

[05:58] Carlos Mendes: i can ping procurement but we also need to make sure the VPC peering is authorized for our test project. i'll validate egress rules and share the security person.

[06:12] Samira Patel: we'll send the SOC2 summary and the security guide after the call. note that some of the security docs are in the shared drive link Alex will include.

[06:25] Leah Kim: small UX Q — if we put a per-route concurrency cap and a queue depth, what does the client see when a request is rejected? can we return a structured JSON code to make backoff deterministic?

[06:38] Samira Patel: yes we return an HTTP 429 with an error code that signals retry-after; we can customize a header for your SDK to interpret.

[06:47] Alex Chen: ok let's go back to the data — Samira, can you walk us through the specific log lines where the p99 spikes occur?

[06:55] Samira Patel: sure, i'll read a snippet — note transcripts often butcher the log field names but the gist: at [run 11] we see a KV fetch miss, which triggers cache load and stalls the request for ~700ms. aggregated effect across many requests pushed p99 up. also we saw occasional syscalls in the host that introduced 30-50ms jitter — we flagged those as noisy neighbors.

[07:25] Priya Rao: noisy neighbors — are those other tenants on the box? we thought the dedicated pool would isolate that.

[07:32] Samira Patel: dedicated reduces cross-tenant noise but doesn't eliminate host-level variance from background OS tasks or networking spikes. we can enable CPU pinning and tighter NUMA controls in the Dedicated config for your pilot.

[07:50] Carlos Mendes: that's helpful. please include CPU pinning option in the config template.

[07:57] Samira Patel: will do. also we'll attach kernel-level metrics so you can correlate.

[08:05] Alex Chen: timeline check — we want the 8-client run and Samira's reconfigured runs by next Tuesday; that matches the action items we put earlier. anything blocking this week?

[08:17] Priya Rao: only blocking if we don't get the anonymized prompt samples by Friday. I'll try to get them by Thursday.

[08:25] Leah Kim: if the 8-client run looks good, what's the path to scale to prod? do we need a Dedicated capacity increase or can we autoscale?

[08:34] Samira Patel: you can start with Dedicated with autoscaling policies and reserved baseline. we recommend a baseline capacity to meet steady-state and autoscale for bursts — that reduces cost. we'll produce a recommended policy based on the upcoming runs.

[08:48] Priya Rao: on cost — Alex, please quantify cost delta for baseline (80ms) vs tuned (40ms + caching).

[08:55] Alex Chen: yes i'll include that in the spreadsheet. I'll show cost per 1M tokens and per-hour for the dedicated pool.

[09:05] Carlos Mendes: one more operational question — if we route bursts to a warm pool as you suggested, how long does it take to spin up new workers? is there cold start?

[09:16] Samira Patel: warm pool is warmed to model weights and can take 10-30s to fully accept traffic depending on model size; cold starts are longer. we have burst capacity options that keep a subset hot for sub-second failover but that costs more. we'll show the tradeoffs in the doc.

[09:33] Leah Kim: ok that's helpful.

[09:36] Alex Chen: any competitor stuff we should note? Priya, you mentioned evaluating Anthropic and Bedrock — will this affect your rollout?

[09:45] Priya Rao: we're still benchmarking a few things; Anthropic had lower latency on some of our small tests but cost was higher; Bedrock is attractive for integration but we prefer Redwood's routing/fallback ideas for multi-tenant control. not decided yet.

[09:58] Samira Patel: noted. we'll include comparison notes at a high level.

[10:05] Alex Chen: last thing — recap and next steps. we agreed: 1) Samira will adjust batching window to 40ms, enable higher KV TTL and CPU pinning in pilot config; 2) Priya will share three anonymized prompt sets; 3) Priya/Carlos will run the 8-client production-like test and upload logs; 4) Alex will send benchmark spreadsheet and security docs. target dates are in the action items.

[10:40] Priya Rao: yep that works. thanks everyone.

[10:45] Carlos Mendes: thanks.

[10:48] Leah Kim: thanks all.

[10:50] Alex Chen: end call — i'll follow up with calendar invite for the deep dive.

End of transcript.
